cells.tense: You are tending what is growing here, and your hands are in the work right now.
cells.ask: Show one person what this has cost so far. Let them see the hours, not just the growth.
cells.core:
You are tending what grows, and you are not forcing it. Enough light for the next step is what the work asks for, and you keep taking that step — watering, mending, turning things toward the sun when they lean. The path keeps revealing itself one bend at a time, and you keep walking it.

Someone should see what this has cost. That is what the care is free to do next: let one person witness the work, not just the harvest. Release comes after completion, and honoring what you put in comes first. Say what you have given, plainly, to one person who can hear it — and let the telling be part of the work.
cells.sheetLine: You tend it honestly, and the work keeps finding its next step.
cells.verb: tending what grows with responsible care
cells.place: moving through uncertainty without forcing clarity

cells.tense: You are tending what has not yet grown, and your hands are already tired from a harvest that is not here.
cells.ask: Leave one thing unattended today on purpose and let it grow without you for a day.
cells.core:
You are tending a garden that has not grown yet. Ahead of you is every version of what this could become, and you are already there — pruning branches that do not exist, planning the plenty, working through the night for a morning that keeps moving. What you give is real. The tiredness comes from carrying a season that has not arrived.

What is being asked of you is smaller: let one thing stay as it is today. Not abandoned — just not handled, while the growing keeps happening without you. When the grip loosens, the picture has room to land. Care that does not exhaust is the face this work is reaching for.
cells.sheetLine: You are caring for a future that has not arrived, and it is wearing you down.

cells.tense: You stopped tending this, and you are standing where you used to tend it.
cells.ask: Put two hands back into one small thing this week — prune, water, mend — in a piece small enough to finish.
cells.core:
Tending what grows is small moves, made steadily — water what needs water, mend what is torn, let the rest keep going on its own. You knew how to do that once, and you did it without needing to see the whole road ahead.

Right now your hands are not in it. You are standing at the door, waiting to know how it will turn out before you come back in. What is asked of you is not a return to all of it. Pick the smallest living thing you have been leaving alone, and put two hands into just that part this week. Strength comes from continuing to hope, not from hoping harder.

cells.tense: You are already tending what grows here, but you call it something else when you talk about it.
cells.ask: Name one piece of this work out loud today and call it yours, not the situation's.
cells.core:
You are already keeping something alive here — deciding where it goes, taking the small steps that hold it together. But when you talk about it, you call it circumstance. You say the thing needed keeping, or life happens, or someone has to. The work is happening, and the credit has not been handed to you by you.

Start with one thing. Name one piece of what you do as yours, out loud, to one person. Care that shows up as steady work deserves to be visible, and the first person it should be visible to is you. That is what this is free to do next.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that this person's care has exhausted them, which the record does not say — the seat's mechanism is navigating ambiguity, and the card is stewardship, so the failure is in how care is held, not its amount. A reader could say the card means caring for land or money, not people, and the cells should stay open to both. The ask survives being wrong: tending one thing carefully and letting one thing stay unfinished is useful whether or not this reading is accurate. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line about 'not choosing between priorities,' which sounds like insight and hands over nothing the person can do.
